article_title: Social Regulation of Learning
citation: Hampton, S., Glazer, K., Dragnić-Cindrić, D., & Fusco, J. (2025). Social Regulation of Learning. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/249
title: Observable indicators distinguish low-quality from high-quality socially shared regulation of learning
description: The primer offers a side-by-side table of observable behaviors so observers "can quickly discern what a student could experience in a classroom environment with low-quality versus high-quality socially shared regulation of learning." Low-quality indicators include sustained off-task behavior, unequal contributions, frequent hostility, and frequent need for teacher intervention; high-quality indicators include balanced contributions, mutual support and respect, and the group working together to overcome challenges.
requirements: Because observing inside a learner's mind is not possible, practical and observable indicators are needed; many indicators are likely to be present simultaneously and intermittently
constraints: Indicators are observational proxies, not direct measures of regulation; the primer notes regulation's impact on learning can be hard to measure
target_learners: K-12 students in group learning
target_learning_goals: Recognizing and fostering socially shared regulation of learning
examples: High-quality student behaviors listed include asking clarifying questions, using reasoning phrases such as "I think X because of Y," managing conflicts without teacher intervention, and referencing additional materials with little or no prompting
key_sources: Hampton, S., Glazer, K., Dragnić-Cindrić, D., & Fusco, J. (2025). Social Regulation of Learning. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/249

article_title: Research and Evaluation on School Safety: The Structure, Services, and Products of State School Safety Centers
citation: McKenna, J. M., Russo, S., Sutherland, H., Muñoz, E., Boal, A., & Petrosino, A. (2023). Research and evaluation on school safety: The structure, services, and products of state school safety centers. WestEd. https://www.ojp.gov
title: Two-phase SSSC activity data collection protocol (Qualtrics survey plus Smartsheet workspaces)
description: The evaluation's activity data collection is a two-phase instrument for retrospectively documenting SSSC services over calendar year 2021. Phase 1 is a Qualtrics survey with 23 questions across five sections covering training events, technical assistance, resources, compliance activities, and grant administration; Phase 2 provides each center a customized Smartsheet workspace for service-level detail. The report states that "Seventeen SSSCs from 16 states completed the Qualtrics survey portion of the activity data collection, and 9 SSSCs from 9 states submitted at least one type of Smartsheet." The interview analysis used a codebook with 33 code families and 208 subcodes.
requirements: Centers must complete the Qualtrics survey before receiving Smartsheets, which are provided based on survey responses about which services the center provides
constraints: Participation in the Smartsheet phase was partial: 9 SSSCs submitted training data, 4 technical assistance data, 9 resources data, 3 compliance data, and 3 grant administration data
target_learners: State school safety center staff
State educational agency staff
target_learning_goals: Documenting and characterizing the services, activities, and outputs of state school safety centers
examples: The training events Smartsheet documented event name, dates, length in hours, description, training type and modality, number and types of participants, topics, presenters, and funding sources
key_sources: McKenna, J. M., Russo, S., Sutherland, H., Muñoz, E., Boal, A., & Petrosino, A. (2023). Research and evaluation on school safety: The structure, services, and products of state school safety centers. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED628907

article_title: The Future of Student Self-Assessment: a Review of Known Unknowns and Potential Directions
citation: Panadero, E., Brown, G. T. L., & Strijbos, J.-W. (2016). The Future of Student Self-Assessment: a Review of Known Unknowns and Potential Directions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9350-2
title: Five SSA typologies framework showing divergent conceptions of self-assessment components
description: The review organizes student self-assessment research around five typologies, which reveal that although researchers hold different conceptions of what SSA's components are, the field still applies SSA in a largely uniform way. The article states that "Five SSA typologies were identified showing that there are different conceptions on the SSA components but the field still uses SSA quite uniformly." This framework serves as the review's first organizing axis and grounds its call for conceptual clarification.
requirements: Researchers and practitioners need to make their conception of SSA components explicit, since the field currently applies SSA uniformly despite divergent typologies
constraints: The typologies were identified from existing literature; the review notes the field still uses SSA quite uniformly despite the differing conceptions
target_learners: students in K-12 and higher education engaging in self-assessment
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment of one's own learning and performance
examples: The review identifies five distinct SSA typologies from prior literature as its first research topic
key_sources: Panadero, E., Brown, G. T. L., & Strijbos, J.-W. (2016). The Future of Student Self-Assessment: a Review of Known Unknowns and Potential Directions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9350-2

article_title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
citation: Panadero E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Front. Psychol. 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422
title: SSRL model: three modes of regulation in collaborative learning (SRL, CoRL, SSRL)
description: The Hadwin, Järvelä and Miller model addresses regulation in collaborative and computer-supported learning. It proposes three modes: individual self-regulation adapting to interaction with group members; co-regulation, which "refers broadly to affordances and constraints stimulating the (student's) appropriation of strategic planning, enactment, reflection, and adaptation"; and socially shared regulation, where "deliberate, strategic and transactive planning, task enactment, reflection and adaptation" emerge through transactive exchanges among group members. SSRL unfolds in four loosely sequenced, recursively linked feedback loops adapted from Winne and Hadwin, extending regulation from the "I" or "you" level to collective activity.
requirements: Group members must commit to group work, establish shared common ground, and negotiate and share task perceptions, strategies and goals
constraints: The CoRL mode's use has not been consistent in the field and it has been the most disputed regulatory level; CoRL and SSRL can both occur as groups progress through different collaboration phases
target_learners: students in collaborative and computer-supported collaborative learning settings
target_learning_goals: shared regulation of group learning
collaborative planning and evaluation
examples: A review by Panadero and Järvelä found empirical evidence of SSRL occurrence in cognitive, metacognitive, motivational and emotional shared areas
key_sources: Panadero E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Front. Psychol. 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422

article_title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
citation: Panadero, E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Frontiers in Psychology, 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422
title: Hadwin, Järvelä, and Miller's SSRL model: three modes of regulation in collaborative learning
description: The socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) model addresses regulation in collaborative settings. The review states the model "proposed the existence of three modes of regulation in collaborative settings: self-regulation (SRL), co-regulation (CoRL), and shared regulation (SSRL)". SSRL occurs when deliberate, strategic and transactive planning, task enactment, reflection and adaptation are taken within a group, extending regulation from the 'I' or 'you' level to collective activity. SSRL unfolds in four recursively linked feedback loops adapted from Winne and Hadwin, and the forthcoming version introduces Winne's COPES architecture.
requirements: Group members must commit to group work, establish shared common ground, and negotiate and share task perceptions, strategies, and goals
constraints: The CoRL mode has been in dispute in the field due to inconsistent use, and CoRL and SSRL may both occur as groups progress through collaboration phases
target_learners: students in computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) settings
target_learning_goals: shared regulation of group learning tasks
examples: Current instruments combine scaffolding and measures in context, such as computer-supported environments promoting group awareness, planning, and evaluation, plus multimodal data including eye tracking and physiological responses
key_sources: Panadero, E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Frontiers in Psychology, 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422

article_title: Capturing the dynamic and cyclical nature of regulation: Methodological Progress in understanding socially shared regulation in learning
citation: Järvelä, S., Järvenoja, H., & Malmberg, J. (2019). Capturing the dynamic and cyclical nature of regulation: Methodological Progress in understanding socially shared regulation in learning. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09313-2
title: Socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) as a group-level regulatory framework alongside self-regulation and co-regulation
description: The article frames regulation in collaborative learning as occurring on an individual–social continuum, where self-regulation (regulating oneself), co-regulation (supporting each other), and socially shared regulation (regulating together) jointly form the relative regulated learning space. It builds on Winne and Hadwin's COPES model of individual SRL cycles, modeling learning as a cyclical process through phases of task perception, goal setting and planning, enacting strategies, and evaluation. SSRL specifically assumes reciprocity: "Socially shared regulation, particularly, assumes reciprocity in regulatory actions between the group members."
requirements: Understanding regulation in social context requires capturing individuals' subjective psychological premises and appraisals simultaneously with interaction processes
constraints: Regulation is not linear but cyclical and temporally fluctuating, making it hard to capture with single-point or retrospective measures
target_learners: students in collaborative learning groups
CSCL participants
target_learning_goals: regulation of cognition, motivation, and emotion during collaborative learning
key_sources: Järvelä, S., Järvenoja, H., & Malmberg, J. (2019). Capturing the dynamic and cyclical nature of regulation: Methodological Progress in understanding socially shared regulation in learning. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09313-2

article_title: ‘Supporting socially shared regulation during collaborative task-oriented reading’
citation: Kielstra, J., Molenaar, I., van Steensel, R., & Verhoeven, L. (2022). 'Supporting socially shared regulation during collaborative task‑oriented reading'. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 17, 65–105. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09365-x
title: Four types of intra-group social metacognitive interaction (ignored, accepted, shared, co-constructed) as a measure of sharedness in socially shared regulated learning
description: The study's framework for socially shared regulated learning (SSRL) distinguishes levels of sharedness by how group members relate to each other's metacognitive contributions. Metacognitive episodes are coded as one of "four types of intra-group social metacognitive interaction: ignored, accepted, shared and co-constructed". Co-construction, where students build on and elaborate on each other's metacognitive activities, is posited to foster meaningful SSRL and potentially improve individual regulation. Depth of regulation is analysed in parallel as low- versus deep-level orientation, planning and reflection.
requirements: Transcribed group discussion coded at utterance level into metacognitive episodes, with changes in topic marking episode boundaries.
constraints: Interrater reliability was moderate to excellent across the four interaction types (K from 0.71 to 0.93), yet co-constructed episodes were rare in this sample.
target_learners: secondary school students working in collaborative reading groups
target_learning_goals: socially shared metacognitive regulation during collaborative task-oriented reading
examples: Table 2 exemplifies co-construction: one student proposes targeted reading, another confirms, and a third adds the reason 'Because you have to look something up'.
key_sources: Kielstra, J., Molenaar, I., van Steensel, R., & Verhoeven, L. (2022). 'Supporting socially shared regulation during collaborative task‑oriented reading'. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 17, 65–105. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09365-x

article_title: Conceptual socialization in debriefing: tactics as an object of knowledge in wargame interactions
citation: Sjöblom, B., & Lymer, G. (2025). Conceptual socialization in debriefing: tactics as an object of knowledge in wargame interactions. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09717-8
title: SSM (Simple Surface Warfare Model) digital wargame platform for teaching naval tactics
description: The Simple Surface Warfare Model (SSM) is a proprietary digital wargame of the Swedish Defence University used in navy and marine tactics courses. The article describes it as "a digital map-based platform, in which a variety of scenarios can be set up", with military units maneuvered in real time and players deciding on sensors and weapons. Games are played by two opposing sides in continuous time, feature fog of war with a dynamically updated situational picture projected on a classroom wall, and range from roughly three-hour small games to multi-week exercises engaging up to 50 students in multilayered task structures.
requirements: Teams of players with computers controlling a dozen or more units, with projected situational picture for joint overview
constraints: Built on openly available data and not classified; the strategic level of warfare is not present in the game
target_learners: navy and marine cadets in the three-year Swedish officers' program
target_learning_goals: identifying and solving tactical problems of increasing complexity
examples: Coastal defense scenarios in the Baltic Sea or fictional geography with asymmetric sides modeled on Swedish and Russian materiel
key_sources: Sjöblom, B., & Lymer, G. (2025). Conceptual socialization in debriefing: tactics as an object of knowledge in wargame interactions. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09717-8

article_title: Sequential patterns of challenges and socially shared regulation of learning: a comparison of pre-service and in-service teachers’ collaborative learning
citation: Faisal Channa, Piia Näykki, Päivi Häkkinen, Kristóf Fenyvesi, Takumi Yada. (2026). Sequential patterns of challenges and socially shared regulation of learning: a comparison of pre-service and in-service teachers’ collaborative learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09818-y
title: Socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) as an emergent, interactionally constructed group process shaped by professional trajectories
description: The study is grounded in the SSRL framework, in which "SSRL, by contrast, is a fully collaborative process in which group members jointly regulate their learning by setting shared goals, monitoring group progress and collectively managing sociocognitive, socioemotional and motivational aspects of learning". SSRL is distinguished from individual self-regulated learning and from co-regulated learning, and is treated as an emergent property of collaboration rather than a stable individual trait. The article further conceptualises professional experience as a contextual condition shaping how regulation is enacted and sequenced, explicitly not as a causal variable determining outcomes.
requirements: All group members must contribute actively to shared regulatory efforts rather than relying on a single dominant group member
constraints: The study does not assume a causal relationship between professional experience and regulatory effectiveness; differences reflect orientations, not superiority
target_learners: pre-service teachers
in-service teachers in professional development
target_learning_goals: collaborative regulation of sociocognitive, socioemotional and motivational aspects of group learning
examples: 22 triads of teachers regulated collaborative Labster simulation tasks while video-recorded, and their coded interactions were modelled as sequential process maps
key_sources: Faisal Channa, Piia Näykki, Päivi Häkkinen, Kristóf Fenyvesi, Takumi Yada. (2026). Sequential patterns of challenges and socially shared regulation of learning: a comparison of pre-service and in-service teachers’ collaborative learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09818-y

article_title: How social challenges affect children’s regulation and assignment quality in hypermedia: a process mining study
citation: Cindy Paans & Erdem Onan & Inge Molenaar & Ludo Verhoeven & Eliane Segers. (2019). How social challenges affect children's regulation and assignment quality in hypermedia: a process mining study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-019-09204-9
title: Socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) and three types of regulation in collaborative settings
description: The article frames collaborative learning through socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL), defined as "the collective and interdependently sharing of regulatory processes, beliefs, and knowledge, in order to arrive at a shared and co-constructed product or learning outcome". Drawing on Järvelä and Hadwin, it distinguishes three types of regulation: self-regulated learning, in which learners regulate independently; co-regulation, in which peers provide temporary support to each other's self-regulation; and SSRL, characterized by "a shared task understanding and by collective goals and strategies". The study uses this framework to interpret how dyads' cognitive, metacognitive, and relational activities jointly regulate group learning in hypermedia.
requirements: Collaborative settings in which dyad members must coordinate cognitive, metacognitive, and relational activities toward a shared product
constraints: The study coded activities at the level of individual turns, so it "could distinguish between cognitive and metacognitive activities, but not between self-regulation, co-regulation, or shared regulation of learning"
target_learners: Primary school children (5th and 6th grade, ages 10–12) working in dyads
target_learning_goals: Collaborative knowledge construction and writing in a hypermedia inquiry task (heart and healthy living)
examples: The study applied the framework to 30 dyads writing a 300-word text in a WebQuest environment, coding verbal interactions for cognitive, metacognitive, relational, and off-task activities
key_sources: Cindy Paans & Erdem Onan & Inge Molenaar & Ludo Verhoeven & Eliane Segers. (2019). How social challenges affect children's regulation and assignment quality in hypermedia: a process mining study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-019-09204-9

article_title: Physiological synchrony amongst medical residents during crisis management simulation training and a video-based assessment of leaders’ performance
citation: Lucia Patino Melo, Sebastian Wallot, Keerat Grewal, Matthew Moreno, Osamu Nomura, Jason M. Harley. (2026). Physiological synchrony amongst medical residents during crisis management simulation training and a video-based assessment of leaders' performance. Learning and Instruction 102 (2026) 102302. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102302
title: Socially shared regulated learning (SSRL) as a lens for team emotional dynamics in simulation
description: The study uses self- and socially-shared regulated learning (SSRL) theory to situate team-level emotional processes in CRM simulation. SSRL concerns collaboratively regulating learning among multiple individuals, requiring teams to "negotiate personal interests, set common goals, and manage the team as members progress in accomplishing these goals". The authors draw on SSRL's proposition that "shared emotional responses can be indicators of adaptive learning" to motivate their hypothesis that physiological synchrony relates to team performance. They note shared monitoring was not measured but helps interpret and situate the findings.
requirements: Team members need baseline understanding of individual regulatory abilities and skills to contribute to team goals; SSRL presupposes prerequisite SRL abilities
constraints: Shared monitoring and other SSRL processes were not measured in this study; the theory is used for interpretation only
target_learners: medical residents working in teams during simulation training
target_learning_goals: collaborative regulation of learning and emotion in high-stakes team performance
examples: The authors use SSRL's shared-emotion proposition to justify expecting PS to positively correlate with leader performance
key_sources: Lucia Patino Melo, Sebastian Wallot, Keerat Grewal, Matthew Moreno, Osamu Nomura, Jason M. Harley. (2026). Physiological synchrony amongst medical residents during crisis management simulation training and a video-based assessment of leaders' performance. Learning and Instruction 102 (2026) 102302. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102302

article_title: Steady-state EEG captures how elementary classroom instruction drives plasticity for novel visual words
citation: Fang Wang, Elizabeth Y. Toomarian, Radhika S. Gosavi, Blair Kaneshiro, Anthony M. Norcia & Bruce D. McCandliss. (2025). Steady-state EEG captures how elementary classroom instruction drives plasticity for novel visual words. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00371-w
title: SSVEP oddball paradigm with reliable components analysis for school-based EEG measurement of word learning
description: A measurement element combining steady-state visual evoked potentials with Reliable Components Analysis (RCA) over a 128-sensor array, recorded in a laboratory inside the school. Word oddballs are presented at 1 Hz within a 3 Hz base stream across three conditions (learned-vs-unlearned low-frequency words, high-frequency words vs pseudowords, medium-frequency words vs pseudowords). The article notes the paradigm elicits much higher signal-to-noise responses than other EEG paradigms, enabling reliable measurement with just 10 trials of 10 s each, and that RCA produces component topographies more closely resembling underlying cortical sources than PCA or Common Spatial Patterns.
requirements: A dedicated EEG recording space within the school; brief practice session; a repetition detection task young readers can sustain; RCA spatial filtering with permutation tests and FDR correction
constraints: Signals above 10 Hz are very weak, so analyses were restricted to frequencies and harmonics within 10 Hz; catch trials were excluded due to movement artifacts from button presses
target_learners: children aged roughly 6.75 to 8.89 years in early elementary grades
target_learning_goals: measuring cortical discrimination of learned versus novel visual word forms
examples: Each participant completed 30 trials total across three conditions in about 40 minutes including setup, practice, and breaks; 8 of 10 trials per condition were used for analysis
key_sources: Fang Wang, Elizabeth Y. Toomarian, Radhika S. Gosavi, Blair Kaneshiro, Anthony M. Norcia & Bruce D. McCandliss. (2025). Steady-state EEG captures how elementary classroom instruction drives plasticity for novel visual words. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00371-w

article_title: The Enhancement of Junior High School Students' Abilities in Mathematical Problem Solving Using Soft Skill-Based Metacognitive Learning
citation: Murni, A., Sabandar, J., Kusumah, Y. S., & Kartasamita, B. G. (2013). The Enhancement of Junior High School Students' Abilities in Mathematical Problem Solving Using Soft Skill-Based Metacognitive Learning. IndoMS-JME, Volume 4, No. 2, July 2013, pp. 194-203. https://jurnal.unila.ac.id/index.php/jme
title: Soft skill-based metacognitive learning follows a five-step lesson sequence
description: The article's SSML approach is enacted as a lesson pattern in which "students follow a leraning by five steps are: early discussion; independence; group discussion; group presentation; and reflection and conclusion." Each step pairs metacognitive activity (planning, monitoring, evaluating thinking in problem solving) with the empowerment of named soft-skill values such as confidence, honesty, independence, and cooperation. The pattern was implemented in experimental classes in the quasi-experimental study.
requirements: Teachers skilled at asking metacognitive questions and observing each student's condition and creativity are described as required when students finish problem-solving questions
target_learners: grade VII junior high school students
target_learning_goals: mathematical problem solving ability
metacognitive behavior
soft skills and character
examples: In the study, three grade VII classes per school were randomly assigned to SSML or conventional learning and taught Social Arithmetic through this five-step sequence.
key_sources: Murni, A., Sabandar, J., Kusumah, Y. S., & Kartasamita, B. G. (2013). The Enhancement of Junior High School Students' Abilities in Mathematical Problem Solving Using Soft Skill-Based Metacognitive Learning. article_title: The Enhancement of Junior High School Students' Abilities in Mathematical Problem Solving Using Soft Skill-Based Metacognitive Learning
citation: Murni, A., Sabandar, J., Kusumah, Y. S., & Kartasamita, B. G. (2013). The Enhancement of Junior High School Students' Abilities in Mathematical Problem Solving Using Soft Skill-Based Metacognitive Learning. IndoMS-JME, Volume 4, No. 2, July 2013, pp. 194-203. https://jurnal.unila.ac.id/index.php/jme
title: Soft skill-based metacognitive learning (SSML) as an approach combining metacognitive awareness with soft-skill empowerment
description: SSML is the article's named framework: "Learning is instill awareness to the student a process of how to design, monitor, and evaluate the thought processes and activities carried out in solving problem." To solve problems, students connect past and present knowledge, use appropriate problem-solving strategies, and reflect on the process and solution, while soft-skill values (religious, self-confident, independent, curious, hard-working, courteous, respectful, honest, cooperative) are empowered throughout. The framework was tested against conventional learning in a quasi-experiment.
requirements: Learning begins with contextual problems involving soft skills to develop mathematical problem-solving skills
target_learners: grade VII junior high school students
target_learning_goals: mathematical problem solving ability
metacognitive awareness in planning, monitoring, and evaluating thinking
character and soft-skill development
examples: The framework was operationalized in the study's five-step lesson sequence and compared with conventional learning across two school levels and three MPK categories.

article_title: Efficacy of the Social Skills Improvement System--Classwide Intervention Program (SSIS-CIP) in the Primary Grades
citation: DiPerna, J. C., Lei, P., Bellinger, J., & Cheng, W. (2014). Efficacy of the Social Skills Improvement System – Classwide Intervention Program (SSIS – CIP) in the Primary Grades. SREE Spring 2014 Conference. https://www.sree.org
title: SSIS Classwide Intervention Program (SSIS-CIP)
description: The SSIS-CIP is the universal component of the Social Skills Improvement System, a program integrating assessment and intervention to improve children's social skills and classroom engagement. It teaches "the 10 social skills that teachers have identified as most critical to classroom success" through a "10-week structured curriculum that includes teacher lesson plans, video vignettes, student workbook activities, progress monitoring, and parent communications." Skills are taught individually in units of three 20-25 minute lessons covering listening to others, following directions, following classroom rules, ignoring peer distractions, asking for help, taking turns in conversations, cooperating, controlling anger, acting responsibly, and showing kindness.
requirements: Delivered classwide by classroom teachers over a 10-week structured curriculum with lesson plans, video vignettes, workbooks, progress monitoring, and parent communications
constraints: Its efficacy in school settings had yet to be determined prior to this trial; effects depend on class pretest levels
target_learners: Primary-grade elementary students (ages ~7) in general education classrooms
target_learning_goals: Social skills supporting classroom success
Academic engagement and motivation
examples: Implemented in 20 randomly assigned classrooms across two Pennsylvania school districts, with fidelity assessed via structured observations
key_sources: DiPerna, J. C., Lei, P., Bellinger, J., & Cheng, W. (2014). Efficacy of the Social Skills Improvement System – Classwide Intervention Program (SSIS – CIP) in the Primary Grades. SREE Spring 2014 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED562704

article_title: The Effects of Conceptual Change Texts Enriched with Metaconceptual Activities on the Symmetry of Classroom Teacher Candidates
citation: Batdal Karaduman, G. (2019). The Effects of Conceptual Change Texts Enriched with Metaconceptual Activities on the symmetry of Classroom Teacher Candidates. Acta Didactica Napocensia, 12(1), 107-116. https://doi.org/10.24193/adn.12.1.7
title: Symmetry Subjects Comprehension Test (SSCT)
description: The data collection tool was a Symmetry Comprehension Test of "28 questions which were prepared by the researcher", with expert opinion consulted during preparation. Its "Cronbach Alpha value of the test was calculated as .70". It was administered as a pre-test before reading the texts and as a post-test after reading them, and SPSS was used for data analysis.
requirements: Expert opinion was consulted during preparation of the test
constraints: Reliability of .70 is reported for this sample of 60 teacher candidates
target_learners: Undergraduate classroom teacher candidates
target_learning_goals: Measuring comprehension of symmetry concepts
examples: Applied as pre-test before students read the texts and as post-test after they read them

article_title: Social-Emotional Learning Program to Promote Prosocial and Academic Skills among Middle School Students with Disabilities
citation: Espelage, D. L., Rose, C. A., & Polanin, J. R. (2016). Social-Emotional Learning Program to Promote Prosocial and Academic Skills Among Middle School Students With Disabilities. Remedial and Special Education, 37(6), 323–332. https://doi.org/10.1177/0741932515627475
title: Second Step–Student Success Through Prevention (SS-SSTP) middle school SEL curriculum
description: SS-SSTP (Committee for Children, 2008) is a middle school SEL curriculum "designed for sixth- through eighth graders" covering "empathy, communication skills, problem-solving, bully prevention, friendship skills, harassment, emotion regulation, alcohol and drug prevention" across grades, with context increasing in complexity from one grade level to the next. Fifteen lessons are delivered in sixth grade and 13 lessons at each of the seventh- and eighth-grade levels, each taking one 50-min session or two 25-min sessions. Teachers received a 4-hr training covering the research rationale, lesson walkthroughs, and fidelity strategies.
requirements: Teacher training prior to implementation, including research review, lesson demonstration, and implementation strategies to maximize fidelity
constraints: The control schools in the analyzed subsample did not adopt the P3R: Stories of Us—Bullying program materials they were provided
target_learners: sixth- through eighth-grade students, including students with disabilities receiving special education services
target_learning_goals: empathy and emotion regulation
communication and problem-solving skills
bully prevention and willingness to intervene
examples: Teachers in intervention schools completed a 4-hr training and were encouraged to prepare lessons ahead of time, prepare lessons as a team, and use provided facilitation tips
key_sources: Espelage, D. L., Rose, C. A., & Polanin, J. R. (2016). Social-Emotional Learning Program to Promote Prosocial and Academic Skills Among Middle School Students With Disabilities. Remedial and Special Education, 37(6), 323–332. https://doi.org/10.1177/0741932515627475

article_title: Results of a Randomized Controlled Trial of Student Success Skills
citation: Webb, L., Villares, E., Carey, J., Wells, C., & Sayer, A. (2014). Results of a Randomized Controlled Trial of Student Success Skills. SREE Fall 2014 Conference. https://sree.org
title: Student Success Skills (SSS) classroom-based intervention
description: SSS is a fully developed structured program in widespread use, designed to systematically teach students fundamental social, emotional, and learning skills. School counselors introduced key skills to all 5th grade students through "five 45-minute classroom lessons in the fall followed by two 45-minute booster lessons in the spring," after which teachers encouraged students to apply the skills to the regular curriculum. Its skills fall into five areas: goal setting and progress monitoring; creating a caring, supportive classroom; cognitive and memory skills; performing under pressure and managing anxiety; and building healthy optimism.
requirements: Implementation by trained school counselors with reinforcement by classroom teachers, supported by a structured manual to increase fidelity of implementation
constraints: In this trial it was evaluated only in 5th grade classrooms in two large Florida school districts
target_learners: 5th grade students in elementary school
target_learning_goals: Cognitive and meta-cognitive skills such as goal setting and progress monitoring
Social skills such as listening and teamwork
Self-management skills such as managing attention, motivation, and anxiety
examples: In the trial, over 10,000 school counselors and teachers had been trained in fifteen states, and fidelity was rated one to three via counselor self-reports and district coordinator site visits; no schools were dropped for low fidelity.
key_sources: Webb, L., Villares, E., Carey, J., Wells, C., & Sayer, A. (2014). Results of a Randomized Controlled Trial of Student Success Skills. SREE Fall 2014 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED562995

article_title: The Outcomes of a Social Skills Teaching Program for Inclusive Classroom Teachers
citation: Elif SAZAK PINAR, Bülbin SUCUOGLU. (2013). The Outcomes of a Social Skills Teaching Program for Inclusive Classroom Teachers. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 13(4), 2247-2261. https://www.edam.com.tr/kuyeb
title: Short-term teacher training combining information, video examples, exercises, and discussion of easy-to-use techniques
description: The SSTP was a six-hour program in four sessions of one and a half hours each, built around presenting information, watching 19 previously recorded real-life classroom videos, doing exercises based on real-life examples, and discussion. It taught five techniques (modeling, rehearsing, prompting, giving cues, rewarding) chosen from observation and interview data about what teachers lacked and wanted. The authors state that "programs similar to the SSTP consisting of many exercises, real- life examples, and visual materials with a short implementation time can be a useful tool for training teachers".
requirements: Content determined based on the needs, interests, and expectations of teachers
Techniques that can be easily implemented in a short period of time, demonstrated step-by-step with clear language
constraints: Effects on student outcomes were not examined in this study
Observational data were gathered in only one academic class
target_learners: Inclusive grade 1-2 classroom teachers in public elementary schools
target_learning_goals: Knowledge of teaching social skills
Use of social skills teaching techniques (modeling, rehearsing, prompting, giving cues, rewarding)
Expectations regarding social skills of students with special needs
examples: Four sessions totaling six hours, twice-weekly in seminar rooms at teachers' own schools, using 19 previously recorded classroom videos depicting social skills difficulties and teacher behaviors
key_sources: Elif SAZAK PINAR, Bülbin SUCUOGLU. (2013). The Outcomes of a Social Skills Teaching Program for Inclusive Classroom Teachers. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 13(4), 2247-2261. https://www.edam.com.tr/kuyeb

article_title: Creative Thinking of Low Academic Student Undergoing Search Solve Create and Share Learning Integrated with Metacognitive Strategy
citation: Yusnaeni, Corebima, A. D., Susilo, H. & Zubaidah, S. (2017). Creative Thinking of Low Academic Student Undergoing Search Solve Create and Share Learning Integrated with Metacognitive Strategy. International Journal of Instruction, 10(2), 245-262. http://www.e-iji.net/dosyalar/iji_2017_2_16.pdf
title: SSCS+MS: Search, Solve, Create and Share cooperative problem-solving learning integrated with underlining and self-assessing metacognitive strategies
description: SSCS is described as "one of the cooperative learning models based on problem solving" with the syntax of Pizzini and Separdson (1992). In this study the metacognitive strategy was implemented by "adding the intervention of researcher in the form of underlining technique in the phase of search and self-assessing at the end of share phase." The authors argue the integration lets students monitor their learning and adapt, fostering self-regulated, independent learning that develops creative thinking.
requirements: Requires the SSCS problem-solving syntax with researcher-added underlining in the search phase and self-assessing at the end of the share phase
constraints: Studied only with tenth-grade natural science classes in three Kupang schools over one semester on biodiversity, virus, protista and monera content
target_learners: tenth-grade students of low and high academic ability in senior high school
target_learning_goals: creative thinking ability
self-regulated learning
examples: Three classes per school were taught traditional learning, SSCS, or SSCS+MS for one semester

Creative Thinking of Low Academic Student Undergoing Search Solve Create and Share Learning Integrated with Metacognitive Strategy. article_title: The Use of Geospatial Technologies Instruction within a Student/Teacher/Scientist Partnership: Increasing Students' Geospatial Skills and Atmospheric Concept Knowledge
citation: Hedley, M. L., Templin, M. A., Czajkowski, K., & Czerniak, C. (2013). The Use of Geospatial Technologies Instruction Within a Student/Teacher/Scientist Partnership: Increasing Students' Geospatial Skills and Atmospheric Concept Knowledge. Journal of Geoscience Education. https://doi.org/10.5408/11-237.1
title: Standardized Spatial Skills (SSK) test measuring geospatial skills in the context of geospatial technologies
description: The SSK test by Lee (2007), published by the Association of American Geographers, measures geospatial skills such as geographic relief, spatial interactions, movements, and distributions/patterns of phenomena as surfaces. Lee and Bednarz (2009) gathered validity evidence including a Pearson correlation of 0.578 between SSK scores and geotechnology coursework completed, and reported reliability of Cronbach's alpha = 0.7034. In the present study, the geospatial skills section showed Cronbach's alpha = 0.845. The article states "The first 16 questions assessed spatial skills in the context of geospatial technologies (Lee, 2007)."
requirements: written permission from the author and publisher for use
constraints: lower reliability for the science section of the test (Cronbach's alpha = 0.607)
target_learners: grades 7-12 students
target_learning_goals: geospatial skills assessment

article_title: Situational simulation teaching can effectively enhance the clinical thinking ability of residents.
citation: Meng Jing, Wang Li, Jin Danni, Li Zihan, Tao Qingqing, Ying Lan. (2025). Situational simulation teaching can effectively enhance the clinical thinking ability of residents. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08248-7
title: SST as a closed-loop 'scenario experience—practical operation—reflection and optimization' learning model for clinical thinking
description: The article frames situational simulation teaching as an immersive approach that replicates highly realistic clinical environments using high-fidelity mannequins, assistant-played family members and nurses, pre-class preparation, a timed scenario with evolving patient deterioration, instructor debriefing, and post-class personalized feedback. The authors state that "SST fosters a 'scenario experience—practical operation—reflection and optimization' closed-loop learning model," positioning it against traditional passive lectures for training decision-making under pressure.
requirements: Senior instructors trained in SST who can independently guide residents
High-fidelity mannequins with externally controlled vital signs and trained teaching assistants to advance the scenario
Structured pre-class materials and quizzes plus post-class evaluation and feedback
constraints: In this study the model was implemented with a single clinical scenario (hypovolemic shock) in one emergency medicine department
target_learners: second-year emergency medicine residents
target_learning_goals: clinical thinking and rapid critical illness assessment
emergency decision-making and team coordination
doctor-patient communication and ethical decision-making
examples: A 25-minute simulated gastrointestinal-bleeding scenario in which the mannequin's SpO2 dropped to 83% and blood pressure to 75/45 mmHg while residents adjusted treatment plans, followed by debriefing
key_sources: Meng Jing, Wang Li, Jin Danni, Li Zihan, Tao Qingqing, Ying Lan. (2025). Situational simulation teaching can effectively enhance the clinical thinking ability of residents. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08248-7

article_title: Psychometric analysis of the Slovak version of the satisfaction with simulation experience scale (measurement invariance).
citation: Polónyiová K., Teličák P., Vitovič P., Hnilicová S. (2025). Psychometric analysis of the Slovak version of the satisfaction with simulation experience scale (measurement invariance). Medical Education Online, 30(1). https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2025.2534055
title: Three-factor structure of simulation satisfaction (debriefing and reflection, clinical reasoning, clinical learning)
description: The SSE scale conceptualises student satisfaction with simulation as a multidimensional construct rather than a single enjoyment rating. The article states the questionnaire "provides data about general student satisfaction with simulation experience and its three components: debriefing and reflection, clinical reasoning, and clinical learning." The CFA in this study confirmed this three-factor structure with high factor loadings (predominantly above 0.800) in both language groups. The authors also relate satisfaction to Kolb's experiential learning, Vygotsky's scaffolding, Bandura's social learning, and Piaget's constructivism, viewing satisfaction as an indicator of pedagogical soundness.
requirements: Administration after a concrete simulation experience; higher scores indicate higher satisfaction
constraints: The scale is not explicitly grounded in a specific learning theory, per the authors
target_learners: health-discipline students, here medical students
target_learning_goals: evaluating satisfaction with simulation-based education as a program-quality indicator
examples: Used to evaluate three newly implemented simulation scenarios added to existing course portfolios
key_sources: Polónyiová K., Teličák P., Vitovič P., Hnilicová S. (2025). Psychometric analysis of the Slovak version of the satisfaction with simulation experience scale (measurement invariance). Medical Education Online, 30(1). https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2025.2534055

article_title: Investigating the role of self-assessment in enhancing self-regulated learning amongst medical students in problem-based learning.
citation: Khoiriyah Umatul, Roberts Chris. (2025). Investigating the role of self-assessment in enhancing self-regulated learning amongst medical students in problem-based learning. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07359-5
title: Self-assessment Scale for Active Learning and Critical Thinking (SSACT)
description: The SSACT is a previously validated self-assessment tool designed specifically for the PBL tutorial context, measuring self-assessment of "active learning and critical thinking" across "two domains and 14 items". Its items "correspond to the activities in all steps of the seven jump tutorial method", so completing it scaffolds students' procedural knowledge of PBL tutorials. Internal consistency was high overall and per domain (Cronbach's α > 0.8). Students completed it three times during the course and tutors provided written feedback based on it.
requirements: Its content must be aligned with the learning activities required in the PBL tutorial context; tutors provide accompanying written feedback
constraints: Developed and evaluated in a first-year medical PBL context at one institution; the article states broader applicability across courses or institutions needs further validity evidence, particularly for educational impact
target_learners: novice medical students in PBL tutorials
target_learning_goals: active learning, critical thinking, and self-regulated learning during tutorial phases of problem analysis, independent study, and reporting
examples: In the study, 90 students completed the SSACT at the end of units 1, 3, and 5 of the neuromusculoskeletal course, with tutors giving written feedback each unit without prior access to students' responses
key_sources: Khoiriyah Umatul, Roberts Chris. (2025). Investigating the role of self-assessment in enhancing self-regulated learning amongst medical students in problem-based learning. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07359-5

article_title: Impact of High-Fidelity Simulation on the Acquisition of Spiritual Competencies in a Nursing Degree in Spain: An Experimental Pre-Post Study.
citation: Domènech-Sorolla, J., Martínez-Rodríguez, L., Pedregosa-Fauste, S., Muns-Orenga, A., García-Díaz, F., & Fernández-Pascual, M. D. (2025). Impact of High-Fidelity Simulation on the Acquisition of Spiritual Competencies in a Nursing Degree in Spain: An Experimental Pre–Post Study. Journal of Religion and Health. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10943-025-02285-8
title: SSCRS-Sp: Spanish-language Spirituality and Spiritual Care Rating Scale for nursing students
description: The SSCRS-Sp is the validated Spanish version for nursing students of McSherry et al.'s Spirituality and Spiritual Care Rating Scale, "consists of 17 items with a 5-point Likert scale response (0 = strongly disagree; 5 = strongly agree), grouped into four dimensions: Spirituality, Spiritual Care, Religiosity, and Personalized Care." It reports Cronbach's alpha = 0.72 in this sample and served as the pre/post outcome measure. It was developed from a literature review and data from 549 clinical nurses in England.
requirements: Respondents complete it before and after the learning activity to detect changes in perceptions
constraints: The scale was validated for nursing students in a separate published validation article
It measures perceptions, not clinical performance
target_learners: Undergraduate nursing students
target_learning_goals: Perceptions of spirituality and spiritual care competencies
examples: Used as pre (Phase 1) and post (Phase 5) questionnaire in the five-phase simulation activity
key_sources: Domènech-Sorolla, J., Martínez-Rodríguez, L., Pedregosa-Fauste, S., Muns-Orenga, A., García-Díaz, F., & Fernández-Pascual, M. D. (2025). Impact of High-Fidelity Simulation on the Acquisition of Spiritual Competencies in a Nursing Degree in Spain: An Experimental Pre–Post Study. Journal of Religion and Health. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10943-025-02285-8

article_title: Situational simulation teaching effectively improves dental students' non-operational clinical competency and objective structured clinical examination performance.
citation: Wu Ju-Hui, Lin Pei Chen, Lee Kun-Tsung, Liu Hsin-Liang, Lu Peih-Ying, Lee Chen-Yi. (2024). Situational simulation teaching effectively improves dental students’ non-operational clinical competency and objective structured clinical examination performance. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05546-4
title: Situational simulation course (SSC) for dental non-operational clinical competency
description: The SSC is a simulation-based intervention training non-operational clinical competency in fifth-year dental students, covering history taking and information giving, oral appliance instruction, image interpretation, and SBAR communication. "Each group of two students participated in four 25-min scenarios (Table 1), which were conducted at the dental clinic (in situ)", with standardized patients working from comprehensive scripts. Stations included managing sudden cardiac arrest, safe wheelchair transfer, and oral hygiene instruction.
requirements: Structured scenarios with standardized patient scripts, briefing before the simulation, and feedback, debriefing, and reflection phases afterward
Supervisor evaluation using five-level entrustment rating scales, with any station at level 2 rated as course failure
constraints: SPs tend to be underutilized due to cost and resource constraints, and prior work identified diminishing effectiveness of SP simulation education over time
target_learners: fifth-year undergraduate dental students during clerkship training
target_learning_goals: patient-centered communication and information giving
clinical decision-making and differential diagnosis
interprofessional communication using SBAR
examples: Four in-situ scenarios at the dental clinic: history taking and differential diagnosis with disabilities, managing sudden cardiac arrest, oral hygiene instruction with oral appliances, and oral care before denosumab injection
key_sources: Wu Ju-Hui, Lin Pei Chen, Lee Kun-Tsung, Liu Hsin-Liang, Lu Peih-Ying, Lee Chen-Yi. (2024). Situational simulation teaching effectively improves dental students’ non-operational clinical competency and objective structured clinical examination performance. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05546-4

article_title: How peer relationships affect academic achievement among junior high school students: The chain mediating roles of learning motivation and learning engagement.
citation: Shao Yanhong, Kang Shumin, Lu Quan, Zhang Chao, Li Ruoxi. (2024). How peer relationships affect academic achievement among junior high school students: The chain mediating roles of learning motivation and learning engagement. BMC Psychology 12, 278. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-024-01780-z
title: Self-system model of motivational development as framework for peer effects on achievement
description: The self-system model of motivational development (SSMMD), proposed by Connell and Wellborn and rooted in self-determination theory, comprises "four interconnected components: social context, self-system, action, and developmental results". The social context, including peers, shapes self-beliefs and motivation; motivation drives engagement in activities; and engagement influences developmental outcomes such as academic performance. The study maps peer relationships to social context, learning motivation to the self-system, learning engagement to action, and academic achievement to developmental outcomes, and reports that the data support this linear pathway.
requirements: The model presumes a linear developmental pathway in which social context influences the self-system, which influences actions and subsequently outcomes
constraints: The article notes the study tentatively demonstrated the applicability of SSMMD in junior high school settings in China
target_learners: junior high school students aged 13–14
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in Chinese, mathematics, and English
examples: The study tested the SSMMD-derived hypotheses with SEM on survey and exam-score data from 717 students
key_sources: Shao Yanhong, Kang Shumin, Lu Quan, Zhang Chao, Li Ruoxi. (2024). How peer relationships affect academic achievement among junior high school students: The chain mediating roles of learning motivation and learning engagement. BMC Psychology 12, 278. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-024-01780-z

article_title: Student standardized patients versus occupational standardized patients for improving clinical competency among TCM medical students: a 3-year prospective randomized study.
citation: Zeng Jinhao, Liang Shuang, Fu Xiaoxu, Guo Jing, Bai Yaolin, Zhou Shan, Du Quanyu, Wang Zhenxing, Zhang Xiyu, Peng Sihan, Wen Lijuan, Li Wenyuan, Li Bin, Yang Han, Zhang Yi. (2023). Student standardized patients versus occupational standardized patients for improving clinical competency among TCM medical students: a 3-year prospective randomized study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04198-0
title: SSP-TCM program: trained TCM postgraduate student standardized patients as a lower-cost simulation alternative
description: The SSP-TCM program recruits voluntary first-year TCM postgraduate students and trains them as standardized patients of TCM through "a systematic training course consisting of didactic sessions and skill practice, and self-study sessions" delivered by senior SP trainers. Of 18 recruits, 15 passed a qualification test assessed by blinded SP instructors and internal medicine specialists. The program ran alongside an existing OSP-TCM program at Chengdu University of TCM, which the authors describe as efficient but costly and time-intensive.
requirements: Voluntary postgraduates with physical and mental fitness based on psychological test files and health examination records; those with acting talent and strong sense of responsibility prioritized
Four months of systematic training and passage of a blinded qualification test before participation
constraints: Graduate student mobility requires retraining new batches as previous SSPs graduate
Age limitations of graduate students make portraying elderly, infant, or pregnant patients difficult
target_learners: Fourth-year TCM undergraduates in clinical competency training
target_learning_goals: TCM clinical competency including history-taking, syndrome differentiation, and doctor-patient communication
examples: In the trial, 10 student standardized patients served the SSP-TCM group, matched by an equal number of occupational standardized patients in the OSP-TCM group over a 10-week, 40-class-hour curriculum
key_sources: Zeng Jinhao, Liang Shuang, Fu Xiaoxu, Guo Jing, Bai Yaolin, Zhou Shan, Du Quanyu, Wang Zhenxing, Zhang Xiyu, Peng Sihan, Wen Lijuan, Li Wenyuan, Li Bin, Yang Han, Zhang Yi. (2023). Student standardized patients versus occupational standardized patients for improving clinical competency among TCM medical students: a 3-year prospective randomized study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04198-0
